title: Copies of Copies: Variants and the Critic's Toolkit
description: Why no originals survive, how scribes err, and how stemmatics sorts the copies

concepts.title: No Autographs, Thousands of Witnesses
concepts.contentHtml:
Start with an uncomfortable fact: not one of the 27 books of the New Testament survives in its author's own copy, and the same is true of every book of the Hebrew Bible. What survives are witnesses: manuscripts copied from earlier manuscripts, ancient translations, and quotations in later writers. Textual criticism is the discipline that compares those witnesses and works back towards the text they descend from.

The numbers are large. The Institute for New Testament Textual Research (INTF) in Münster puts the extant Greek manuscripts at about 5,700, most of them copied in the second millennium.1 The earliest papyrus fragments come from the second century, and the first complete copies, the great parchment codices Vaticanus and Sinaiticus, from the fourth. No two manuscripts agree exactly. Each has its own variant profile, and each place where witnesses differ is a variation unit.

How many variants are there? Peter Gurry offered the first estimate with a stated method in 2016. He counted every difference in wording among Greek manuscripts, ignoring spelling, and arrived at roughly half a million.2 That sounds alarming until you look inside the number. More than half of those variants occur in a single manuscript, and many are nonsense slips. Gurry argues that the total reflects how often the text was copied more than how carelessly it was copied.3 The INTF makes a similar point: in most places only one or a few manuscripts stray from a reliable majority, and a significant split in the tradition occurs in about ten per cent of the variation units.4

Not everyone reads those facts the same way. Bart Ehrman's bestseller Misquoting Jesus (2005), subtitled The Story Behind Who Changed the Bible and Why, brought the scale of variation to a mass audience. Gurry, an evangelical scholar, replies that a small group of hard cases, such as Jesus's prayer from the cross in Luke 23:34, matter for interpretation, yet he knows of no difficult variant that by itself determines Christian doctrine. Both sides use the same evidence; they disagree about what it means.

concepts.title: How Scribes Go Wrong, and How Critics Catch Them
concepts.contentHtml:
Most variants have ordinary causes, and critics sort them into families. The Encyclopaedia Judaica lists the classic copying slips: repeating the same word twice (dittography), omitting one of two similar adjacent letters or words (haplography), and missing words or lines because the same word occurs further on1 (homoioteleuton, "same ending"). In that last case the eye jumps from one occurrence to the next and everything between drops out. Copying from dictation added errors of hearing, such as Hebrew eilav, "unto him", written for el av, "unto father".

Other changes were deliberate, or at least thoughtful. The INTF recalls that Jerome complained that scribes often copied the text not as it stood in their exemplars but as they understood it,2 and many variants look like attempts to correct what a scribe took to be a mistake. Scribes smoothed grammar, filled in a familiar phrase from a parallel passage (harmonisation) or added a clarifying word.

From these habits critics drew rules of thumb. The most famous is lectio difficilior potior: other things being equal, the harder reading is preferable, because a scribe is more likely to replace an unusual word with a common one than the reverse. Its companion, lectio brevior potior ("the shorter reading is stronger"), assumes scribes added more often than they cut, although homoioteleuton shows that a shorter text can simply be a damaged one.

Can a rule of thumb be tested? In 2010 three researchers at Cornell and Ithaca College treated Karl Lachmann's celebrated 1850 edition of Lucretius as a natural experiment. They argued that scribal errors tend to replace rarer, more information-rich words with commoner ones, which is exactly the habit the rule assumes.3 Across 756 places where Lachmann chose between two grammatically acceptable readings, his choices ran towards the rarer word, and a later edition by Ernout accepted 547 of them, or 72 per cent.4 A careful editor, in the language of information theory, can recover meaningful signal from noisy copying.

concepts.title: Family Trees of Manuscripts
concepts.contentHtml:
Counting manuscripts is a trap: a hundred late copies of one exemplar are really a single witness. Stemmatics tries instead to reconstruct the family tree, the stemma codicum. Karl Lachmann is usually credited with turning the idea into a systematic method, although his principles are scattered through the introductions to his editions; the classic formulation came from Paul Maas.

The method rests on shared errors. If two manuscripts share a mistake that copyists would not easily make independently, they probably descend from a common ancestor that already contained it. Grouping manuscripts by such errors yields the tree, and the tree tells the editor which readings are independent evidence. The method as formulated by Maas uses common errors to decide whether manuscripts are related,1 and it insists on two stages: recensio, working out the relationships and the lost archetype at the top of the tree, and only then emendatio, correcting the archetype where it is still corrupt.

Real traditions resist tidy trees. Scribes often compared copies and corrected one against another, so readings crossed between branches. This contamination blurs the tree. One of the strongest objections came from Giorgio Pasquali, who disagreed with the supposition that every textual tradition must descend from a single archetype and showed how little the method achieves when applied strictly.2

Biblical traditions are among the most contaminated of all, with thousands of manuscripts and centuries of cross-checking. That is why Gerd Mink at the INTF developed the Coherence-Based Genealogical Method (CBGM). Editors decide the direction of change at each variation unit in a small local stemma, and a computer then measures how coherently each witness relates to every other across the whole text. Peter Gurry notes that the method was designed to address contamination and coincidental agreement, and it has become an essential tool for the editors of the standard Greek New Testament.3 Other scholars borrow software from evolutionary biology, such as the PHYLIP package, to draw unrooted trees; Katarzyna Kapitan argues that this lets us treat the stemma as a research tool rather than the final product of an edition.4

title: Three Ancient Witnesses to the Hebrew Bible
description: The Masoretic Text, the Septuagint and the Samaritan Pentateuch, and how they differ

concepts.title: The Masoretes and the Crown of Aleppo
concepts.contentHtml:
The Hebrew Bible read in synagogues, and printed in most editions today, is the Masoretic Text (MT), named after the Masoretes, the scholars who guarded it in the early Middle Ages. Their predecessors were already obsessive about exactness: the Talmud says the early sages were called soferim because they counted all the letters of the Torah. The Masoretes went further and fixed how the text was to be read aloud. Hebrew had been written with consonants only. The vowel points and accent marks came later, and the Encyclopaedia Judaica concludes that these signs were not introduced before the sixth century.1 Around the text the Masoretes wrote the Masorah, marginal notes recording unusual spellings, counts and even the middle verse of the Torah, so that a copyist could check his work.

The jewel of the tradition is the Aleppo Codex, known as the "Crown", and treated as Judaism's most authoritative Bible from the moment it was made, around 930 CE. It was probably the first single volume containing every book of the Hebrew Bible. The scribe Shlomo ben Buya'a copied the consonants, and Aharon ben Asher, the most outstanding of the Masoretes of Tiberias, added the vowels, accents and notes.2 Maimonides later based his rules for writing Torah scrolls on it.

Its modern history reads like a thriller. The codex was damaged in 1947 during anti-Jewish riots in Aleppo. When it reached Israel at the beginning of 1958, nearly two hundred folios, about 40 per cent, were missing, including much of the beginning and end.3 Most of the sheets from Deuteronomy 28:17 to the Song of Songs survived. The journalist Matti Friedman later found that the accepted story of its rescue did not add up, and what became of the lost leaves is still uncertain.

The other great witness is the Leningrad Codex (B19a), written in 1009, whose vowels were adjusted to Ben Asher's system, as its colophon states.4 Precious as they are, both codices are medieval, copied well over a thousand years after the books they contain were written.

concepts.title: The Septuagint: A Greek Window on a Lost Hebrew
concepts.contentHtml:
Long before the Masoretes, Greek-speaking Jews in Egypt translated their scriptures. The name Septuagint (LXX, "seventy") comes from a legend in the Letter of Aristeas: 72 translators sent from Jerusalem to Alexandria produced the Greek Pentateuch in the reign of Ptolemy II Philadelphus (285–246 BCE).1 The miraculous details are legend, but the time and place fit what is known of Hellenistic Judaism. The other books followed over some four centuries, from the early third century BCE to the early second century CE.

Why does a translation matter for the Hebrew text? Because a translation is a witness to its source. Where the Greek differs from the MT, critics ask whether the translator paraphrased, misread, or faithfully rendered a different Hebrew original, which they call the Vorlage. The most dramatic case is Jeremiah. The Septuagint version is one-eighth shorter than the Masoretic one.2 It was long put down to a poor translation. Then Hebrew manuscripts of both the longer and the shorter forms turned up among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and the "bad translation" became evidence for two Hebrew editions of the book.

The Greek text has its own history of revision. Later Jewish translators such as Aquila and Symmachus produced fresh Greek versions, and the Christian scholar Origen (died 254) set versions side by side in his Hexapla. Disentangling the original Greek from these later layers is a specialist field of its own.

The Septuagint is also scripture in its own right. Early Christians read it, the New Testament writers quote it, and together with the Greek New Testament it is still the official Bible of the Greek Orthodox Church.3 For many Orthodox readers, then, a Septuagint reading is not merely a variant to weigh against the Hebrew; it is the church's own text. Rabbinic Judaism, by contrast, came to treat the Masoretic tradition as authoritative. A critic can treat both as witnesses, while each community may reasonably ask which text is its Bible.

concepts.title: The Samaritan Pentateuch
concepts.contentHtml:
A third ancient witness belongs to a living community. The Samaritans, who hold Mount Gerizim to be God's chosen place, preserve their own Hebrew Torah. The first copy to reach Western scholars was obtained in Damascus by Pietro della Valle in 1616, and hopes ran high that it would reveal a text older than the MT.1 In 1815, however, Gesenius sorted its roughly 6,000 differences from the MT into eight classes, among them grammatical revision, explanatory glosses, readings borrowed from parallel passages and larger additions.2 His verdict that the MT was older and better held sway for a century.

Some differences are plainly sectarian. After the Ten Commandments the Samaritan text adds a long passage built mainly from Deuteronomy 27 and 11:30, and it is generally agreed that this was inserted to support the claim that Gerizim is "the chosen place".3 Yet the suspicion can run both ways: R. H. Pfeiffer, among others, thought Judean scribes may in turn have minimised biblical support for the Samaritan temple. The Samaritans hold that their treasured Abisha Scroll was written by Abisha son of Phinehas in the 13th year after the conquest of Canaan; scholars generally agree it cannot be earlier than the twelfth century CE.

The real surprise is how often the Samaritan text agrees with the Septuagint against the MT. At Genesis 4:8 both give Cain's words to Abel, "Let us go out into the field", which the MT lacks. At Exodus 12:40 both count the 430 years of sojourn to include the patriarchs' time in Canaan. Still, in most cases the Samaritan text sides with the MT against the Greek.

Then came Qumran. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, some biblical fragments clearly resemble the Samaritan text-type.4 Beneath its sectarian additions, then, the Samaritan Pentateuch preserves a form of the Torah that was already circulating among Jews in the last centuries BCE. Gesenius was right that many of its readings are secondary, but its basic text is older than he allowed.

title: The Dead Sea Scrolls and a Plural Bible
description: What the Qumran caves revealed about stability, fluidity and the idea of an original

concepts.title: Eleven Caves
concepts.contentHtml:
In late 1946 or in 1947, three Bedouin wandering along the north-west shore of the Dead Sea stumbled on a cave containing ten jars.1 All but two were empty; one held dirt, and the other held what proved to be the Great Isaiah Scroll, together with a rule book for a religious community and a commentary on Habakkuk. Nearly a year passed before scholars learned of them. The search that followed, by Bedouin and archaeologists alike, turned up ten more caves around the ruins of Khirbet Qumran, the last in 1956.

The haul is about 930 manuscripts, most surviving only as fragments, dating from the third century BCE to the first century CE. Each has a siglum, in which Q stands for Qumran: 4Q169 is the 169th manuscript from Cave 4, and 1QIsaᵃ is the first Isaiah scroll from Cave 1. Hebrew dominates, but about 15 per cent are in Aramaic and a few in Greek. About 230 are biblical scrolls, copies of books now in the Hebrew Bible, and every book is represented except Esther.2 About a dozen are even written in paleo-Hebrew, the script of the First Temple era.

Who owned them is still argued over. Early scholars attributed the whole collection to the Essenes, a Jewish sect described in ancient sources. That consensus has since been challenged and modified, although many scholars still see a link. About a quarter of the non-biblical texts are "sectarian", describing the beliefs and rules of a particular community; others, such as Jubilees, were widely read Jewish works previously known only in translation.

For textual critics the biblical scrolls changed everything. The Great Isaiah Scroll is 7.34 metres long and contains 54 columns of Hebrew; it is traditionally dated to the late second century BCE. Overnight, the oldest Hebrew witness to Isaiah became more than a thousand years older.

concepts.title: Stable Text, Fluid Text
concepts.contentHtml:
The first lesson of the scrolls was reassuring. Many biblical manuscripts closely resemble the Masoretic Text, which is remarkable given that they are over a thousand years older than any biblical manuscript known before.1 In large stretches, generations of scribes had copied with real care, and the consonantal text behind the medieval codices turned out to be ancient. Scholars call that ancestor the proto-Masoretic text.

The second lesson was unsettling. Other scrolls differ from the MT in language and spelling, and some contain additions and deletions suggesting that their scribes felt free to modify what they copied.2 Some fragments resemble the Samaritan text-type, and the Hebrew copies of Jeremiah include both the long form found in the MT and the short form behind the Septuagint. In the Second Temple period, in other words, different forms of the same book could circulate side by side.

The most debated example is a Samuel scroll from Cave 4, 4QSamᵃ. It often agrees with the Septuagint, though its text also contains clearly proto-Masoretic elements. Before 1 Samuel 11 it has a paragraph found in no Masoretic manuscript: Nahash, king of the Ammonites, has been gouging out the right eyes of the men of Gad and Reuben, and seven thousand men have fled to Jabesh-Gilead. Without that paragraph, Nahash's demand in verse 2 to put out the right eye of every man in Jabesh comes out of nowhere.

Is the paragraph original, accidentally lost from the MT, or a later expansion that explains the story? Lawrence Schiffman notes that the historian Josephus knew the passage, so it was at least part of some Jews' text of Samuel in Second Temple times, and he thinks it may belong to the original book.3 He also stresses that it stands alone. Most additions in the Qumran biblical scrolls are explanatory expansions, the products of interpretation rather than lost originals, so each case has to be argued on its merits.

concepts.title: Which Text Is the Bible?
concepts.contentHtml:
The scrolls force a question that sounds simple: what exactly are textual critics trying to recover? For a single author's work the obvious answer is the author's text. But if Jeremiah circulated in a short and a long edition, both in Hebrew, which one is "the original"? If the shorter is an earlier edition that was later expanded, the Masoretic Jeremiah is not a corrupted text but a later, fuller stage of the book's growth.

Scholars therefore distinguish several possible targets. One is the author's original. Another is the archetype, the latest common ancestor of all surviving copies. A third is the initial text, a term coined by Gerd Mink for New Testament work. Peter Gurry shows that even editors who use the term have disagreed about it, and argues that Mink consistently meant the text from which the extant tradition originated.1 That could be the author's text, an archetype or a later edited edition, so each editor must say which.

The canon was settling at the same time as the text. The Israel Antiquities Authority notes that the communities behind the scrolls had no unified idea of an authoritative collection of scriptures; the notion of a closed biblical canon emerged later.2 Even the proto-Masoretic text still shows some fluidity in Judean Desert manuscripts from the first centuries CE, and only afterwards does a single consonantal text prevail.3

Communities of faith answer the question of the "real" text in different ways. For rabbinic Judaism, the Masoretic tradition, embodied in the Aleppo Codex, has long been the authoritative text, and it is the text of most printed Hebrew Bibles. For the Greek Orthodox Church, the Septuagint is the official Old Testament. The Samaritans keep their own Torah. A historian can treat all of these as stages in one long story. A believer must also decide which stage carries authority, and that is a theological judgement the manuscripts alone cannot make.

title: Papyri, Codices and the Greek New Testament
description: The earliest papyri, Codex Sinaiticus, and the fight over which Greek text to print

concepts.title: Papyri and the Problem of P52
concepts.contentHtml:
New Testament manuscripts fall into four main groups. When Peter Gurry wrote in 2016, the official Münster list held 127 papyri, 286 majuscules, 2,841 minuscules and 2,384 lectionaries.1 The papyri are the earliest group, mostly fragments; majuscules are parchment books written in capitals; minuscules are later books in a joined lower-case hand; and lectionaries arrange readings for church services. The list keeps growing as new items are catalogued.

The most famous papyrus is a small scrap in the Rylands collection in Manchester, P.Ryl. iii.457, known as P52. It preserves a few lines of John 18. For decades it anchored the dating of John's Gospel. A respected commentary, quoted by Brent Nongbri, said palaeographers had dated it to the second quarter of the second century (125–150), so John must have been written and circulating in Egypt no later than the first decade of that century.2

Nongbri's articles of 2005 and 2020 challenge that chain of reasoning. The popular date, "about 125 AD", rests entirely on palaeography, the comparison of handwriting with dated specimens, and handwriting cannot deliver that precision.3 Reviewing the comparisons, he argues that the range of possible palaeographic dates for P52 extends into the third century.4 His aim is methodological: he wants scholars to stop using P52 to fix the date of John, not to cast doubt on the papyrus itself.

Not every papyrologist accepts so wide a range, and the debate is a model of how evidence and interpretation interact. A date from handwriting is a judgement about style, and the more precise it sounds, the more it should be questioned. The final lesson of this topic shows how radiocarbon dating and machine learning are now being combined to put such judgements on a firmer footing.

concepts.title: Codex Sinaiticus and the Endings of Mark
concepts.contentHtml:
The oldest complete New Testament survives in a book copied in the second quarter of the fourth century:1 Codex Sinaiticus. It once held the entire Old and New Testaments in Greek, plus two works that did not stay in the canon, the Shepherd of Hermas and the Epistle of Barnabas. It is written four columns to the page in a clear, regular hand. Together with Codex Vaticanus, it is one of the oldest copies of the scriptures on parchment, and both preserve a very early level of the text.

How it left St Catherine's Monastery at Mount Sinai is still disputed. On his first visit, in 1844, the German scholar Constantin Tischendorf took 43 leaves, which remain in Leipzig.2 On his third visit, in 1859, he asked to take the codex to Russia to prepare an edition and, in the monastery's account, promised to return it at the monks' first request. Instead it stayed with the Russian government, which sold it to Britain in 1933 for £100,000; most of it is now in the British Library. Tischendorf justified himself by writing that the monks were about to burn the codex. The monastery has always called that a slander, and it still laments the loss.3

Sinaiticus is central to one of the New Testament's best-known puzzles. The Gospel of Mark has four different endings in the manuscripts. In Sinaiticus and Vaticanus it stops at 16:8, with the women at the empty tomb. Some manuscripts add a short report of the risen Jesus sending out his disciples. Most have the longer ending, 16:9–20, which the Council of Trent accepted as inspired Scripture, and one manuscript in Washington expands even that. Clement of Alexandria and Origen show no knowledge of the longer ending, and Eusebius and Jerome say it was missing from almost all the Greek copies they knew.4 Did Mark mean to stop at 16:8, or was his ending lost? Scholars still disagree, and some argue that the abrupt close is deliberate.

concepts.title: Received, Majority or Critical Text?
concepts.contentHtml:
Which Greek text should a Bible be translated from? Three answers compete. The Textus Receptus ("received text") is the family of printed editions based mainly on Erasmus, named after an advertising blurb in the Elzevir brothers' edition of 1633; it lies behind the King James Version. The critical text descends from B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort's edition of 1881, which argued that the Byzantine text, the form found in most late manuscripts, is secondary.

For much of the twentieth century the Textus Receptus seemed finished: in 1926 A. T. Robertson declared it "as dead as Queen Anne".1 Yet, as Daniel Wallace documented in 1994, a small but growing group revived the view that the original text is found in the majority of manuscripts. Its roots go back to John Burgon, dean of Chichester, whose views rested on verbal inspiration and the doctrine he drew from it, providential preservation. Edward Hills, in The King James Version Defended (1956), defended the Textus Receptus itself. Others edited a Majority Text: Z. C. Hodges and A. L. Farstad, and in 1991 William Pierpont and Maurice Robinson, whose edition reinstates the majority readings for the story of the woman taken in adultery (John 7:53–8:11).2

The critical text has moved on too. The Editio Critica Maior for the Catholic Letters, edited with the CBGM, now forms the basis of the Nestle-Aland 28 and UBS5 editions.3 A famous test case is the Johannine Comma, the Trinitarian words in 1 John 5:7–8 ("in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit"). It is absent from all the ancient Greek manuscripts; only four late ones, from the 13th to 16th centuries, contain it, and the earliest Latin manuscript with it dates from the ninth century.4 The Catholic Church's own path is telling. In 1897 the Holy Office cautioned scholars against rashly doubting the passage; in 1927 it clarified that they may doubt or reject its authenticity.

title: The Synoptic Problem and Q
description: Why Matthew, Mark and Luke overlap, and the case for and against a lost source

concepts.title: Seeing Together
concepts.contentHtml:
Lay Matthew, Mark and Luke side by side and you see what J. J. Griesbach saw when he printed them in parallel columns in his Synopse of 1774,1 giving us the word synoptic, "seeing together". Virtually all of Mark appears in Matthew or Luke or both. The three share distinctive vocabulary and details, and they tell their episodes in much the same order. Explaining those agreements, and the disagreements, is the synoptic problem.

Some early answers appealed to a common source outside the texts: Lessing in 1777 proposed a lost primitive gospel, Schleiermacher in 1817 a set of written fragments, and Herder in 1796 a shared oral tradition. Most scholars now reject such solutions because the verbal agreement is too detailed.2 In places the Greek matches word for word, which points to literary dependence: one evangelist copying another.

But who copied whom? Augustine took Matthew to be first, Mark to be a summary of Matthew, and Luke to depend on both. Griesbach proposed that Mark came last, condensing Matthew and Luke. The Griesbach hypothesis was revived in the 1970s by W. R. Farmer and others, and its favourite example is Mark 1:32. There Mark's "that evening, at sunset" looks like a combination of Matthew's "that evening" and Luke's "when the sun was setting".

Most scholars, however, conclude that Mark came first, and the argument from order carries much of the weight. Matthew, Mark and Luke follow the same sequence of episodes only when Matthew and Luke agree with Mark, as though each were following Mark independently.3 The Griesbach view also struggles to explain why a later Mark would leave out so much of Matthew, including the birth stories and the Sermon on the Mount. Markan priority is therefore the working assumption of most of the field, and a standard Catholic reference work notes that the two-source solution built on it prevails among most scholars, Catholics included.

concepts.title: Q: The Gospel Nobody Has Seen
concepts.contentHtml:
Markan priority explains the material shared by all three gospels, the triple tradition. It leaves a puzzle. Matthew and Luke also share about two hundred verses that are not in Mark,1 the double tradition, mostly sayings of Jesus such as the Lord's Prayer and the Beatitudes. These sometimes agree word for word and in the same order, so they cannot have arisen independently. In 1863 H. J. Holtzmann formally stated the two-source hypothesis:2 Matthew and Luke each used Mark plus a lost collection of sayings, later called Q, from the German Quelle, "source".

No manuscript of Q exists. It is reconstructed from the double tradition, and its standard edition, the Critical Edition of Q by James M. Robinson, Paul Hoffmann and John S. Kloppenborg (2000), cites it by Luke's chapter and verse, because Q specialists think Luke kept Q's order better while Matthew spread it through his gospel. The result is an unusual text: very little narrative, apparently no passion story, and over 90 per cent sayings attributed to Jesus. Some scholars even dig for layers inside it. Kloppenborg argued that wisdom-style instructions on discipleship form its earliest stage and that prophetic warnings of judgement on "this generation" were added later.

Could such a gospel have existed? Two discoveries made the genre look less exotic. In December 1945, Egyptian peasants near Nag Hammadi found a jar holding thirteen leather-bound codices.3 Among them was the Coptic Gospel of Thomas, a collection of Jesus's sayings without any narrative, in the manner of the book of Proverbs. And among the Dead Sea Scrolls, the wisdom text 4QInstruction shows that Jewish instruction literature could carry an apocalyptic outlook, as Q does. Neither find proves that Q existed, but together they anchor it in kinds of literature that really were written.4

concepts.title: Dispensing with Q?
concepts.contentHtml:
A minority of scholars think Q is unnecessary. If Luke had read Matthew, the double tradition needs no lost source at all. The Farrer-Goulder hypothesis keeps Markan priority but has Luke using both Mark and Matthew.1 Its best-known recent champion, Mark Goodacre, argues that none of the standard objections to it holds, that Luke could plausibly have rearranged Matthew's sayings to suit his own aesthetic, and that features of Luke's "Q" passages betray Matthew's editing.

The key evidence for this view is the minor agreements: places where Matthew and Luke agree with each other against Mark in passages that Mark also contains.2 If Matthew and Luke worked independently, each coincidence needs its own explanation; if Luke knew Matthew, they are simply Luke echoing Matthew. Supporters of Q reply that the minor agreements are a small share of the data, and that, weighed against the evidence for Markan priority, they hardly warrant abandoning the two-source hypothesis.

Q's defenders have answered Goodacre in detail. John Kloppenborg replied in 2003 that Goodacre's assumptions about Luke's taste are open to serious objection, and that his argument from Luke 3–7 ultimately cuts against his own case.3 Paul Foster, the same year, tested whether it was really possible to dispense with Q. They also point to the "Mark-Q overlaps", where Matthew and Luke keep both versions of a saying or prefer a non-Markan one, as a sign that Q was older than Mark. A 2024 Bible Odyssey survey still calls the two-source hypothesis the most popular solution, while acknowledging the alternatives.4

Ancient tradition adds its own voice. Eusebius preserves the statement of Papias, bishop of Hierapolis, that "Matthew collected the oracles in the Hebrew language", which some take as a hint of an early Aramaic Matthew. Most scholars doubt that Papias can tell us more than the texts themselves. The question remains open, and that is instructive in itself: a hypothesis can dominate a field for more than a century and a half and still be argued over.

title: The Qur'an's Manuscript History
description: From recitation to codex: the Uthmanic text, the Birmingham leaves and the Sana'a palimpsest

concepts.title: From Recitation to Codex
concepts.contentHtml:
The Qur'an began as speech. Muslim tradition holds that Muhammad received the revelations between 610 and 632, the year of his death, and that they were first preserved in "the memories of men", with parts written on parchment, stone, palm leaves and the shoulder blades of camels. According to the same tradition, the first caliph, Abu Bakr, ordered the material collected into a book, and the third caliph, Uthman, fixed its final authoritative written form in about 650.1 Muslims believe that the Qur'an read today is the same text standardised under Uthman.2

That written form is the rasm, the consonantal skeleton of the text. Early Arabic script left many letters undotted and wrote no short vowels, so one rasm could be voiced in more than one way. Over the following centuries a system of recognised readings (qirāʾāt) grew up, each passed down through named authorities; a classical scheme counts seven. Within the tradition, recitation governs writing: priority is given to recitation and memorisation, and the written page serves them.

Two of these transmissions dominate print today. As Adrian Brockett showed in his 1985 thesis, one stems from Kufa and the other from Medina, and they are known by their second-century transmitters, Hafs and Warsh. Printed copies everywhere except West and North-West Africa follow Hafs, so Hafs is the text of the vast majority of printed Qur'ans.3 Brockett documented the differences between the two as a step towards a critical apparatus of the Qur'an.

Modern printing fixed the picture further. The edition prepared in Cairo under the auspices of al-Azhar, dated by tradition to 1924 though its colophon gives 1919, became the model for later printings.4 The Saudi Medina muṣḥaf launched in 1985 follows it except for two letters.5 When people say that the Qur'an reads the same everywhere, they usually have this printed tradition in mind. The historian's question is how far back that uniformity goes.

concepts.title: The Birmingham Leaves
concepts.contentHtml:
In July 2015 the University of Birmingham announced a remarkable result. Two parchment leaves in its Mingana Collection, written in an early Arabic script called Hijazi and containing parts of suras 18 to 20, had been radiocarbon dated at a laboratory in Oxford. The parchment fell between 568 and 645 CE at the 95.4 per cent level.1 For many years the leaves had been bound in with a similar Qur'an manuscript from the late seventh century; only when they were separated and tested did their age emerge.2

Muhammad is generally thought to have lived from about 570 to 632. Professor David Thomas concluded that the animal whose skin became the parchment was probably alive during the Prophet's lifetime or shortly afterwards, so the text on it could be dated, with some confidence, to less than two decades after his death.3 He added that these portions must have been very close to the form of the Qur'an read today, which supports the view that the text has undergone little or no alteration. The university presented the leaves as being of global significance to Muslim heritage and the study of Islam.

Read the numbers carefully, though. Radiocarbon dates the death of the animal, not the moment of writing, so the writing could be somewhat later than the skin. A range that begins in 568 also starts before the revelations are traditionally said to have begun in 610. That shows the limits of the method, not an early Qur'an: a 77-year window cannot resolve events a few years apart. The fair summary is that the leaves are very early, their text is very close to the Qur'an read today, and they fit the traditional chronology, though the dating alone cannot prove every detail of it.

concepts.title: The Sana'a Palimpsest and the Sceptics
concepts.contentHtml:
Among the manuscripts discovered in 1972 in the Grand Mosque of Ṣanʿāʾ in Yemen is a palimpsest, a manuscript whose first text was washed off so that the parchment could be reused. A later Qur'an was written over the erased one. The lower text, the scriptio inferior, is still faintly visible, and it is something rare: the only known surviving witness to a non-Uthmanic textual tradition of the Qur'an, datable to around the middle of the seventh century.

Behnam Sadeghi and his colleagues published studies and an edition of the lower text, with Uwe Bergmann in Arabica in 2010 and with Mohsen Goudarzi in Der Islam in 2012. Sadeghi and Bergmann describe a Qur'an dating from the first half of the seventh century that does not belong to the Uthmanic tradition.1 They compare it with the codices that tradition attributes to other Companions of the Prophet, such as Ibn Masʿūd, in order to shed light on the prototype behind them all.2 On this view, Uthman's text was one of several closely related early versions, and comparing them brings scholars nearer to the Prophet's own time.

These finds bear on a long argument. In the late 1970s John Wansbrough took the most sceptical position of all. Distrusting the chains of transmission behind early Islamic reports, he applied literary analysis to the Qur'an and other early texts and concluded that none was earlier than the end of the second or beginning of the third Islamic century, roughly two hundred years after Muhammad.3 Seventh-century manuscripts such as those from Birmingham and Ṣanʿāʾ are very hard to square with so late a fixing of the text.

The evidence does not simply close the debate, however. The Ṣanʿāʾ lower text shows that a different text form existed alongside Uthman's, and historians still argue about how and how quickly one form became the standard. For many Muslims, the preservation of the Qur'an is a matter of faith; for historians it is a question for the manuscripts. The earliest leaves are evidence that both can examine, even when they read it differently.

title: New Eyes on Old Texts
description: Multispectral imaging, virtual unwrapping, radiocarbon dating and AI handwriting analysis

concepts.title: Light Beyond the Visible
concepts.contentHtml:
Parchment was costly, so medieval scribes recycled it. They took an old book apart, scraped and washed the ink off its leaves, and wrote a new text over the old. The result is a palimpsest, and the erased layer often survives as a faint ghost under the new writing. St Catherine's Monastery at Sinai, built between 548 and 565 and the world's oldest continually operating monastery, holds more than 160 of them, some with erased texts from as early as the fourth century.1

From 2011 the Sinai Palimpsests Project brought multispectral imaging to bear on them. Each leaf is photographed under illumination at different wavelengths of light, and the images are processed to bring out information the naked eye cannot see. By early 2017 the work had revealed some 6,800 hidden pages in 74 palimpsests.2 "We have identified erased texts in 10 languages that date from the fifth to the 12th centuries," said the project director, Michael Phelps. The languages include Greek, Syriac, Georgian, Arabic, Christian Palestinian Aramaic, Latin, Armenian, Slavonic, Ethiopic and Caucasian Albanian, and some of the erased texts survive in no other form. Before the project, only three of the Sinai palimpsests had been thoroughly studied and published.3

The same technology now protects as well as reveals. The Israel Antiquities Authority, working with Google, set out to image its entire collection of about 930 Dead Sea Scroll manuscripts in high resolution and multiple spectra for the Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library.4 The images reduce the need to expose the fragments to handling and allow conservators to monitor them non-invasively. For textual critics the gain is twofold: letters invisible in older photographs can become legible, and anyone online can check an editor's reading against the evidence.

concepts.title: Unwrapping Without Unrolling
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1970 archaeologists excavating the ancient Jewish community at En-Gedi found, inside the Holy Ark of its synagogue, charred lumps of what looked like parchment scrolls. The settlement had been destroyed by fire around 600 CE, and the fragments had turned to chunks of charcoal that crumbled every time they were touched.1 For some forty years nobody could read them, and physical intervention was unthinkable.

In 2016 a team led by the computer scientist Brent Seales of the University of Kentucky, with scholars including Emanuel Tov, published a solution. They scanned one lump using X-ray micro-computed tomography, then ran a software pipeline they call virtual unwrapping. It has three stages. Segmentation finds the rolled layers inside the 3D scan; texturing assigns brightness values from the scan to those surfaces, so letters appear; and flattening turns the curved surface into a readable 2D image. The ink showed up because it was denser than the parchment, which suggests it contains a metal such as iron or lead, although its exact composition is unknown because no exposed ink could be sampled.2

The scroll is the book of Leviticus, the earliest copy of a Pentateuchal book ever found in a Holy Ark. Radiocarbon dating places it in the third or fourth century CE, while the palaeographer Yardeni suggested the first or second century on the basis of the handwriting.3 As far as it has been deciphered, its text is completely identical with the consonantal framework of the medieval Masoretic Text.4 That matters, because Judean Desert manuscripts from a century or two earlier still show some fluidity in the proto-Masoretic text. En-Gedi catches the standard text after it had settled.

The authors present the method as a new pathway for discoveries buried within damaged materials. Charred, crushed or fused objects in museum stores are no longer necessarily lost; they may simply be waiting for the right scanner and software.

concepts.title: Counting Atoms, Measuring Handwriting
concepts.contentHtml:
Palaeography, dating manuscripts and identifying scribes by their handwriting, has always rested on expert judgement. Two studies led by Mladen Popović of the University of Groningen try to make that judgement measurable. In 2021 his team applied pattern recognition and artificial intelligence to the Great Isaiah Scroll, whose 54 columns look as if one hand wrote them. Without assuming anything about who wrote what, the analysis separated columns from the first and second halves of the scroll, with a clear transition at columns 27–29. That is exactly where the scroll shows a physical seam: a three-line gap at the bottom of column 27 and a change of sheet. The study concluded that two main scribes, closely mirroring each other's style, shared the work, and that the second wrote more variably.

In 2025 the same group introduced Enoch, a date-prediction model trained on 24 scroll samples dated by radiocarbon. Before dating, the samples were chemically treated to remove fatty materials, and their remaining lipid content was checked so it would not skew the dates. Enoch reproduced the radiocarbon dates with mean errors of about 28 to 31 years, and its predictions for 135 undated scrolls agreed with palaeographers' own evaluation in 79 per cent of cases. Both the radiocarbon ranges and Enoch's predictions often came out older than traditional palaeographic estimates.

One result stands out. A copy of Daniel 8–11 from Cave 4, known as 4Q114, has a calibrated radiocarbon range of 230–160 BCE. Critical scholars date the final part of Daniel, on literary-historical grounds, to the 160s BCE, so the copy overlaps the period in which they think the book was completed. Readers who hold a much earlier, traditional date for Daniel are not refuted by this, since a copy can only show when a book already existed. What the result does show is how quickly the book was being copied. The machines do not replace judgement; they make judgements testable.
